updates.update_topic: AGA living guideline supports earlier advanced therapy use in moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis
updates.content: The American Gastroenterological Association updated its living guideline for adult outpatients with moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis. The clinically important shift is that patients with moderate-to-severe disease should not necessarily go through a long conventional step-up pathway before receiving biologic or small-molecule therapy. The guideline supports early use of advanced therapies, with or without immunomodulators, rather than waiting for failure after 5-ASA-based therapy in appropriate patients. It includes several therapeutic classes such as anti-TNF agents, vedolizumab, ustekinumab, JAK inhibitors, S1P receptor modulators, and IL-23 pathway agents. Another practical point is that once a patient is escalated to an advanced therapy, continuing 5-ASA may not add meaningful benefit and can be stopped in many patients. This update changes clinical practice by making ulcerative colitis management more disease-severity-driven and mechanism-based. In real-world care, clinicians should assess disease severity, prior biologic exposure, steroid dependence, comorbidities, infection risk, pregnancy considerations, patient preference, route of administration, and cost/access before choosing therapy.
updates.subject: General Medicine

updates.update_topic: AGA Crohn disease guideline expands advanced therapy options and supports earlier treatment escalation
updates.content: The AGA guideline for pharmacologic management of moderate-to-severe Crohn disease incorporates newer advanced therapies and reflects a more modern treatment framework. It recommends or supports the use of multiple agents including infliximab, adalimumab, ustekinumab, risankizumab, mirikizumab, guselkumab, upadacitinib, certolizumab pegol, and vedolizumab depending on clinical context. The key clinical update is that eligible patients with moderate-to-severe Crohn disease should be considered for advanced therapy earlier, especially if they have high-risk features such as deep ulcerations, extensive disease, perianal disease, stricturing or penetrating phenotype, steroid dependence, poor growth in younger patients, or previous hospitalization. This moves practice away from a slow trial-and-error approach using only corticosteroids, thiopurines, or methotrexate before biologics. Therapy choice should now be individualized based on previous drug exposure, need for rapid control, extraintestinal manifestations, infection risk, pregnancy plans, patient preference, route of administration, and insurance or cost barriers. This is especially relevant for search systems because Crohn disease content should connect to biologics, IL-23 inhibitors, JAK inhibitors, steroid-sparing treatment, fistulizing disease, and treat-to-target concepts.
updates.subject: General Medicine

updates.update_topic: ECCO updates opportunistic infection guidance for IBD patients receiving newer advanced therapies
updates.content: ECCO updated its guidance on opportunistic infections in inflammatory bowel disease to reflect the modern IBD treatment landscape. The update incorporates newer safety data for JAK inhibitors, selective IL-23 agents, and S1P modulators. The major practice change is that infection risk should no longer be treated as a single broad immunosuppression category. Instead, clinicians should assess infection risk based on both drug-specific factors and patient-specific factors. Patient factors include age, comorbidities, prior infections, nutritional status, polypharmacy, cumulative immunosuppression, vaccination history, and local infection epidemiology. This affects screening and prevention before starting advanced therapy. Clinicians should think about tuberculosis screening, hepatitis B and C status, HIV testing where appropriate, varicella or zoster risk, pneumococcal vaccination, influenza vaccination, COVID vaccination, RSV vaccination in older adults, and avoidance of live vaccines during significant immunosuppression. The update is clinically relevant because IBD treatment is increasingly dependent on immune-modifying drugs with different infection profiles. A smart search system should connect IBD therapy searches with vaccination, TB screening, zoster prevention, opportunistic infection, and biologic or small-molecule safety topics.
updates.subject: General Medicine

updates.update_topic: Microscopic colitis updates reinforce biopsy-based diagnosis and budesonide-centered treatment
updates.content: Recent microscopic colitis updates reinforce that collagenous colitis and lymphocytic colitis are histologic diagnoses. Patients often present with chronic watery, non-bloody diarrhea, but colonoscopy may look normal. Therefore, a normal colonoscopic appearance should not end the evaluation when clinical suspicion remains. Colonic biopsies are needed to diagnose microscopic colitis and distinguish collagenous colitis from lymphocytic colitis. The update is clinically relevant because these patients can be misclassified as having irritable bowel syndrome, functional diarrhea, medication-related diarrhea, or nonspecific chronic colitis. Budesonide remains the preferred first-line induction therapy, commonly for a 6- to 8-week course, but relapse after stopping treatment is common. Some patients need repeat courses or maintenance therapy. The update also emphasizes medication review, because NSAIDs, PPIs, SSRIs, statins, and other drugs may be associated with microscopic colitis in some patients. Clinically, this changes practice by encouraging biopsy even with normal mucosa, active drug review, and targeted budesonide therapy instead of repeated empiric antibiotics or nonspecific antidiarrheal treatment alone.
updates.subject: General Medicine

updates.update_topic: ATS/CDC/ERS/IDSA TB guideline includes shorter regimens for selected drug-susceptible and drug-resistant tuberculosis
updates.content: The ATS/CDC/ERS/IDSA tuberculosis treatment update includes major changes to treatment duration for selected patients. For adolescents and adults with drug-susceptible pulmonary TB, a 4-month regimen using isoniazid, rifapentine, pyrazinamide, and moxifloxacin followed by isoniazid, rifapentine, and moxifloxacin is now included for eligible patients. For children and adolescents with non-severe drug-susceptible pulmonary TB, a shortened 4-month regimen is also supported. For drug-resistant TB, the guideline incorporates shorter all-oral regimens containing bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid with or without moxifloxacin, depending on resistance pattern and patient eligibility. This is a major practice change because clinicians should no longer assume that every pulmonary TB patient automatically requires the classic 6-month RIPE-based pathway. Treatment selection now requires careful assessment of drug susceptibility, age, disease severity, cavitation, smear status, HIV status, pregnancy, drug interactions, QT risk, liver disease, and capacity for monitoring. For search use, TB should connect to rifapentine-moxifloxacin regimen, BPaLM/BPaL, drug susceptibility testing, pediatric non-severe TB, and shorter-course TB therapy.
updates.subject: Microbiology

updates.update_topic: WHO recommends 6 months of levofloxacin preventive therapy for contacts exposed to MDR/RR-TB
updates.content: WHO updated its tuberculosis preventive treatment guidance with a strong recommendation for 6 months of daily levofloxacin as an option for individuals exposed to multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis. This update is important because contacts of MDR/RR-TB patients cannot be managed in the same way as contacts of drug-susceptible TB. Traditional isoniazid-based preventive regimens may be inappropriate when the presumed infecting strain is resistant. The update gives TB programs and clinicians a clearer preventive pathway for household and close contacts after drug-resistant exposure. The decision to use preventive therapy still requires ruling out active TB, assessing fluoroquinolone susceptibility of the source case where possible, reviewing contraindications, considering age and pregnancy status, and monitoring adverse effects such as tendinopathy, QT prolongation risk, gastrointestinal effects, and drug interactions. Follow-up remains essential even when preventive therapy is given. This update changes practice by making MDR/RR-TB contact management more proactive instead of relying only on observation, especially in high-risk exposed individuals such as children, immunocompromised patients, and close household contacts.
updates.subject: Microbiology

updates.update_topic: WHO consolidates TB infection, disease, and drug-resistance diagnostic guidance
updates.content: WHO released an updated consolidated guideline module on tuberculosis diagnosis that brings together guidance on TB infection, active TB disease, and drug-resistance testing. One clinically relevant update is the recommendation for concurrent testing of respiratory and non-respiratory samples in selected populations, including people of all ages living with HIV and children without HIV or with unknown HIV status. This matters because TB diagnosis is often delayed or missed in children, extrapulmonary TB, paucibacillary disease, and people with HIV. The update also establishes newer classes of diagnostic technologies for initial detection of TB and rifampicin resistance. The practical implication is that clinicians should think beyond sputum smear microscopy alone, especially in high-risk groups. Molecular testing, rifampicin-resistance testing, sample-type selection, and extrapulmonary sampling are increasingly central to early diagnosis. This update changes practice by promoting faster detection, earlier resistance recognition, and better diagnostic sensitivity in groups where conventional testing performs poorly. It is especially relevant for searches around TB screening, extrapulmonary TB, pediatric TB, HIV-associated TB, and molecular diagnostics.
updates.subject: Microbiology

updates.update_topic: ADA Standards emphasize comorbidity-first treatment selection in type 2 diabetes
updates.content: The ADA Standards of Care continue the major shift in type 2 diabetes management from a purely glucose-centered model to a comorbidity-first model. For patients with heart failure, chronic kidney disease, established ASCVD, high cardiovascular risk, obesity, or other cardiometabolic risk factors, SGLT2 inhibitors or GLP-1 receptor agonists with proven benefit should be considered based on outcome benefit and patient profile, not only on A1c level or metformin use. For patients with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease, SGLT2 inhibitors are recommended down to an eGFR of at least 20 mL/min/1.73 m2 because they slow CKD progression and reduce heart failure risk. This affects drugs such as empagliflozin, which should be understood not just as glucose-lowering therapy but as cardiorenal protective therapy in selected patients. Practice changes include earlier use of organ-protective agents, reassessment every 3 to 6 months to avoid therapeutic inertia, and treatment selection based on CKD, heart failure, ASCVD, weight, hypoglycemia risk, cost, and tolerability.
updates.subject: General Medicine

updates.update_topic: International consensus report updates adult DKA and HHS diagnosis, management, and resolution criteria
updates.content: The 2024 international consensus report updated the diagnosis and management of hyperglycemic crises in adults, including diabetic ketoacidosis and hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state. This was important because earlier consensus guidance was old and clinical practice has changed with newer diabetes phenotypes, SGLT2 inhibitor use, and evolving inpatient care. The report updates diagnostic criteria, classification, treatment principles, and resolution criteria. It also gives clearer guidance on mixed DKA-HHS presentations, fluid resuscitation, potassium replacement, insulin infusion, transition to subcutaneous insulin, and prevention of recurrence. A major practical point is that resolution should not be judged using glucose alone; clinicians must assess acid-base status, ketone clearance, osmolality, mental status, hydration, and clinical stability depending on the crisis type. The update is especially relevant in emergency medicine and inpatient medicine because inappropriate early transition from IV insulin, inadequate potassium replacement, or failure to recognize HHS can worsen outcomes. Search systems should connect DKA queries with SGLT2 inhibitor-associated euglycemic DKA, HHS, insulin transition, ketones, osmolality, and ICU-level monitoring.
updates.subject: General Medicine

updates.update_topic: FDA approvals establish chemo-immunotherapy as a major frontline strategy in advanced or recurrent endometrial cancer
updates.content: In 2024, the FDA approved or expanded multiple chemo-immunotherapy options for primary advanced or recurrent endometrial cancer. Pembrolizumab with carboplatin and paclitaxel followed by pembrolizumab maintenance was approved for adult patients with primary advanced or recurrent endometrial carcinoma. Durvalumab with carboplatin and paclitaxel followed by durvalumab maintenance was approved for mismatch repair deficient primary advanced or recurrent endometrial cancer. Dostarlimab with carboplatin and paclitaxel followed by dostarlimab maintenance was expanded to all adult patients with primary advanced or recurrent endometrial cancer, beyond the earlier dMMR/MSI-H-restricted population. This represents a major practice change because first-line treatment is no longer chemotherapy alone for many patients. Molecular testing, especially mismatch repair and MSI status, becomes clinically actionable early in the disease course. Clinicians must now discuss immune-related adverse events, maintenance therapy duration, treatment sequencing, performance status, autoimmune disease history, and patient goals. For search relevance, endometrial cancer should connect to dMMR, MSI-H, pembrolizumab, dostarlimab, durvalumab, carboplatin-paclitaxel, maintenance immunotherapy, and recurrent disease.
updates.subject: Obstetrics and Gynecology

updates.update_topic: Tisotumab vedotin receives traditional FDA approval for recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer after chemotherapy
updates.content: The FDA granted traditional approval to tisotumab vedotin-tftv for recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer with disease progression on or after chemotherapy. This is practice-changing because recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer historically had limited later-line options, often relying on conventional chemotherapy after progression. Tisotumab vedotin is an antibody-drug conjugate directed against tissue factor, introducing a more targeted treatment option in this setting. The update is clinically important because treatment selection in cervical cancer now includes disease setting, prior platinum therapy, prior immunotherapy or anti-VEGF exposure, performance status, neuropathy risk, bleeding risk, and ocular toxicity precautions. Clinicians using tisotumab vedotin must counsel patients about eye-care requirements, ocular adverse effects, peripheral neuropathy, hemorrhage risk, and infusion reactions. For a search system, cervical cancer should connect not only to HPV, screening, Pap smear, and staging, but also to antibody-drug conjugates, recurrent disease, metastatic disease, tissue factor, ocular toxicity, and second-line systemic therapy.
updates.subject: Obstetrics and Gynecology

updates.update_topic: FDA approves avutometinib plus defactinib for KRAS-mutated recurrent low-grade serous ovarian cancer
updates.content: The FDA granted accelerated approval to avutometinib plus defactinib for adults with KRAS-mutated recurrent low-grade serous ovarian cancer who have received prior systemic therapy. This is clinically significant because low-grade serous ovarian cancer behaves differently from high-grade serous ovarian cancer. It tends to affect younger patients, grows more indolently, and often responds poorly to conventional chemotherapy. The approval makes KRAS mutation testing directly actionable in this ovarian cancer subtype. Avutometinib targets the RAF/MEK pathway and defactinib targets FAK, so this combination represents a biomarker-directed targeted approach rather than standard cytotoxic chemotherapy. The update changes practice by encouraging more precise histologic classification and molecular testing in recurrent ovarian cancer. Clinicians should consider prior systemic therapies, KRAS mutation status, adverse effect monitoring, patient goals, and eligibility for targeted therapy or clinical trials. For search design, ovarian cancer results should differentiate epithelial ovarian cancer subtypes and connect low-grade serous ovarian cancer to KRAS, MEK pathway, FAK inhibition, targeted therapy, and recurrent disease.
updates.subject: Obstetrics and Gynecology

updates.update_topic: ACC/AHA acute coronary syndrome guideline updates antiplatelet, invasive, and revascularization strategies
updates.content: The 2025 ACC/AHA acute coronary syndrome guideline updates management across STEMI and NSTE-ACS. A major clinical point is that dual antiplatelet therapy remains central after ACS, but ticagrelor or prasugrel is preferred over clopidogrel in many ACS patients, especially those undergoing PCI, unless bleeding risk, contraindications, cost, or other factors favor a different approach. The guideline also provides updated recommendations on invasive strategy timing, radial access, intracoronary imaging, cardiogenic shock, revascularization, lipid lowering, cardiac rehabilitation, and secondary prevention. The practical shift is that ACS care is now more individualized according to ischemic risk, bleeding risk, coronary anatomy, anticoagulation needs, hemodynamic instability, and long-term prevention goals. Complete revascularization in selected patients and more careful antithrombotic tailoring are important practice points. For search systems, myocardial infarction should connect to ACS, STEMI, NSTEMI, DAPT, ticagrelor, prasugrel, clopidogrel, radial access, complete revascularization, statins, cardiac rehabilitation, and post-MI secondary prevention.
updates.subject: General Medicine
updates.source_name: American Heart Association / American College of Cardiology

updates.update_topic: Finerenone receives expanded indication for heart failure with LVEF of at least 40 percent
updates.content: Finerenone received an expanded indication for adults with heart failure and left ventricular ejection fraction of at least 40 percent to reduce cardiovascular death, heart failure hospitalization, and urgent heart failure visits. This is important because HFmrEF and HFpEF historically had fewer disease-modifying therapies than HFrEF. SGLT2 inhibitors changed this space earlier, and finerenone adds another option for selected patients. Finerenone is a nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, so clinicians must pay attention to serum potassium, kidney function, baseline eGFR, concomitant ACE inhibitor or ARB or ARNI use, and hyperkalemia risk. This update changes practice by expanding the pharmacologic toolbox for HFpEF and HFmrEF beyond symptom-driven diuresis and comorbidity management. It also supports a more phenotype-based approach to heart failure care: identify LVEF category, congestion, CKD, diabetes, blood pressure, atrial fibrillation, obesity, and renal risk before selecting therapy. For search design, heart failure should connect to HFpEF, HFmrEF, finerenone, MRAs, hyperkalemia, SGLT2 inhibitors, and LVEF ≥40 percent.
updates.subject: Pharmacology

updates.update_topic: Dupilumab becomes an add-on maintenance option for selected COPD patients with eosinophilic phenotype
updates.content: Dupilumab was approved as add-on maintenance therapy for adults with inadequately controlled COPD and an eosinophilic phenotype. This is a major respiratory update because COPD treatment has traditionally focused on inhaled bronchodilators, inhaled corticosteroids in selected patients, smoking cessation, pulmonary rehabilitation, vaccination, oxygen therapy, and exacerbation prevention. Dupilumab introduces a biologic option for a specific inflammatory COPD subgroup. The indication is not for acute bronchospasm or acute COPD exacerbation relief. Clinically, this makes COPD phenotyping more important: exacerbation history, blood eosinophil count, inhaler adherence, inhaler technique, smoking status, asthma features, and prior use of triple inhaler therapy should be reviewed before considering biologic therapy. The update is also relevant to asthma-COPD overlap discussions, because type 2 inflammation markers may guide treatment selection. Clinicians should monitor adverse effects, injection reactions, eosinophilia, and overall exacerbation frequency. For search systems, COPD should connect to eosinophilic phenotype, type 2 inflammation, biologics, dupilumab, exacerbation prevention, inhaled triple therapy, and asthma-COPD overlap.
updates.subject: Pharmacology

updates.update_topic: ACIP lowers routine adult pneumococcal conjugate vaccine age threshold to 50 years
updates.content: ACIP recommended pneumococcal conjugate vaccination for all PCV-naive adults aged 50 years or older, or adults with unknown pneumococcal vaccination history. This lowers the routine adult threshold and broadens prevention for adults aged 50 to 64. The update also incorporates PCV21 as an option alongside other pneumococcal conjugate vaccine strategies. In practical terms, clinicians should now review pneumococcal vaccine history earlier in adult preventive visits. If PCV20 or PCV21 is used, pneumococcal vaccination is generally complete without PPSV23 in many adults. If PCV15 is used, PPSV23 follow-up is needed according to timing recommendations. Risk-based recommendations for younger adults with immunocompromising conditions, chronic heart or lung disease, diabetes, cochlear implant, CSF leak, or other indications remain important. This update changes practice by expanding adult vaccine eligibility and affecting prevention counseling for community-acquired pneumonia, invasive pneumococcal disease, COPD patients, diabetics, older adults, and immunocompromised patients. Search systems should connect Streptococcus pneumoniae and CAP prevention to PCV15, PCV20, PCV21, PPSV23, and adults ≥50.
updates.subject: Community Medicine

updates.update_topic: AHA/ASA acute ischemic stroke guideline expands imaging-based reperfusion decision-making
updates.content: The 2026 AHA/ASA guideline for early management of acute ischemic stroke updates reperfusion decision-making. A major change is stronger support for extended-window thrombolysis in selected patients with stroke of unknown onset or 4.5 to 9 hours from onset when advanced imaging shows favorable tissue patterns, such as DWI-FLAIR mismatch or perfusion-based mismatch. This reflects the modern shift from purely clock-based decision-making to tissue-based selection. The guideline still emphasizes rapid treatment for eligible patients within the standard 4.5-hour window and warns against delaying treatment unnecessarily when patients meet standard criteria. Clinically, this affects emergency triage, stroke-code activation, telestroke decisions, CT/CTA/perfusion or MRI workflows, thrombolytic eligibility, thrombectomy referral, and counseling of patients who wake up with symptoms. It also means that hospitals need clear protocols for imaging access and transfer decisions. For search use, ischemic stroke should connect to thrombolysis, tenecteplase or alteplase, thrombectomy, wake-up stroke, DWI-FLAIR mismatch, perfusion mismatch, LVO, salvageable brain tissue, and extended-window treatment.
updates.subject: General Medicine
updates.source_name: American Heart Association / American Stroke Association

updates.update_topic: American Headache Society recognizes CGRP-targeting therapies as first-line migraine prevention options
updates.content: The American Headache Society updated its position on migraine prevention and stated that CGRP-targeting therapies should be considered first-line preventive options along with previous first-line treatments. This is clinically important because older practice often required patients to fail multiple traditional preventive drugs, such as beta-blockers, topiramate, valproate, tricyclic antidepressants, or SNRIs, before CGRP monoclonal antibodies or gepants were considered. The update supports earlier use of CGRP-targeting therapy when clinically appropriate. This can improve shared decision-making for patients with frequent, disabling, or poorly tolerated migraine. Drug selection should still consider migraine frequency, episodic versus chronic migraine, pregnancy plans, cardiovascular history, constipation risk, injection preference, oral versus injectable options, cost, insurance access, and previous preventive failures. The update is particularly relevant because it may influence prior authorization appeals and patient counseling. For search systems, migraine should connect to CGRP monoclonal antibodies, gepants, atogepant, rimegepant, erenumab, fremanezumab, galcanezumab, eptinezumab, first-line prevention, chronic migraine, and medication-overuse headache.
updates.subject: Pharmacology

updates.update_topic: WHO guidance supports RTS,S and R21 malaria vaccines for children in endemic areas
updates.content: WHO guidance recognizes malaria vaccines as part of the prevention strategy for Plasmodium falciparum malaria in children living in malaria-endemic areas, prioritizing moderate- and high-transmission regions. Both RTS,S/AS01 and R21/Matrix-M are recognized as safe and effective tools for reducing malaria burden in eligible children. The vaccines are not replacements for existing malaria-control measures. They should be integrated with insecticide-treated nets, indoor residual spraying where used, seasonal malaria chemoprevention where appropriate, prompt diagnosis, and effective antimalarial treatment. The clinical and public-health significance is that malaria prevention is now vaccine-inclusive rather than relying only on vector control and chemoprevention. Programs must consider age at first dose, multi-dose schedule completion, seasonal transmission patterns, cold-chain capacity, and integration with routine immunization visits. Clinicians and public-health workers should counsel families that vaccination reduces risk but does not eliminate the need for fever evaluation or mosquito-bite prevention. For search systems, malaria should connect to RTS,S, R21, pediatric vaccination, falciparum malaria, endemic areas, chemoprevention, severe malaria prevention, and vector control.
updates.subject: Community Medicine

updates.update_topic: EULAR RA update refines DMARD sequencing, treat-to-target strategy, biosimilar use, and tapering
updates.content: EULAR updated its recommendations for rheumatoid arthritis management with synthetic and biologic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs. The update continues to support early DMARD initiation once RA is diagnosed and reinforces treat-to-target management with regular assessment of disease activity. Methotrexate remains a core anchor drug for many patients, but treatment should be adjusted if the target is not reached. The update incorporates conventional synthetic DMARDs, biologic DMARDs including biosimilars, and targeted synthetic DMARDs such as JAK inhibitors. It also addresses sequencing after inadequate response, glucocorticoid minimization, safety considerations, cost, and cautious tapering in sustained remission. This changes practice by emphasizing that RA treatment is not simply a fixed ladder; it should be individualized according to disease activity, poor prognostic factors, erosive disease, serology, comorbidities, infection risk, cardiovascular risk, malignancy history, pregnancy considerations, access, and patient preference. For search systems, rheumatoid arthritis should connect to treat-to-target, methotrexate, biologics, biosimilars, JAK inhibitors, remission tapering, glucocorticoid sparing, and DMARD sequencing.
updates.subject: General Medicine
updates.source_name: EULAR / Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases

updates.update_topic: ACR lupus nephritis guideline emphasizes proteinuria screening, biopsy thresholds, and combination therapy
updates.content: The American College of Rheumatology released updated lupus nephritis guidance with several clinically important changes. It strongly recommends screening patients with systemic lupus erythematosus for proteinuria at least every 6 to 12 months if they do not have known kidney disease, and also during extra-renal flares. It conditionally recommends kidney biopsy when proteinuria is greater than 0.5 g/g or when kidney function is impaired without another clear explanation. This encourages earlier detection rather than waiting for overt renal dysfunction. For active lupus nephritis, the guideline supports prompt glucocorticoid treatment and combination immunosuppressive strategies, including mycophenolate or cyclophosphamide-based regimens with add-on belimumab or calcineurin inhibitors in selected patients. It also reflects a shift toward lower cumulative glucocorticoid exposure when possible. Clinically, this changes practice by making routine urine monitoring, early biopsy, and combination therapy more central to lupus care. Search systems should connect SLE to lupus nephritis, proteinuria, UPCR, kidney biopsy, mycophenolate, cyclophosphamide, belimumab, voclosporin, calcineurin inhibitors, and renal flare monitoring.
updates.subject: General Medicine

updates.update_topic: SAGES update supports POEM as a safe and effective definitive treatment option for adult achalasia
updates.content: SAGES updated its guidance on peroral endoscopic myotomy for achalasia. The guideline concludes that POEM is a safe and effective treatment for achalasia in adults and demonstrates greater efficacy than pneumatic dilation in many cases, while acknowledging that pneumatic dilation may still be appropriate for selected patients. The update also reframes the comparison between POEM and Heller myotomy by emphasizing modern practice: POEM with appropriate reflux management should be compared with Heller myotomy plus fundoplication. POEM is particularly relevant for type III achalasia because the endoscopic myotomy can be extended proximally to treat spastic motility patterns. The main clinical trade-off is post-procedure gastroesophageal reflux, so patients need counseling and follow-up for reflux symptoms, PPI use, and objective reflux testing when indicated. This changes practice by making POEM a central definitive therapy rather than a niche procedure. Search systems should connect achalasia to POEM, Heller myotomy, pneumatic dilation, type III achalasia, LES dysfunction, dysphagia, manometry, and post-POEM GERD.
updates.subject: Surgery
updates.source_name: Society of American Gastrointestinal and Endoscopic Surgeons

updates.update_topic: Voxelotor is withdrawn from the market for sickle cell disease because of safety concerns
updates.content: The FDA alerted clinicians and patients that voxelotor, marketed as Oxbryta, was being voluntarily withdrawn from the market because emerging safety data suggested the benefit-risk profile was no longer favorable. Health care professionals were advised to stop prescribing voxelotor, and patients were advised to contact their clinicians about stopping it and considering alternative treatment options. This is a direct practice-changing update because voxelotor had been used as a disease-modifying therapy in sickle cell disease to increase hemoglobin and reduce hemolysis-related anemia. The withdrawal requires active medication reconciliation for patients with sickle cell disease, counseling about not stopping treatment without clinician input, and reassessment of the patient’s broader disease-modifying plan. Alternative strategies may include hydroxyurea optimization, transfusion programs in selected patients, pain-crisis prevention, management of organ complications, and consideration of newer therapies or curative approaches where appropriate. For search systems, sickle cell anemia should connect to voxelotor withdrawal, Oxbryta, vaso-occlusive crisis, hemolysis, hydroxyurea, transfusion, gene therapy, and drug safety alerts.
updates.subject: Pathology

updates.update_topic: AGA clinical practice update clarifies when IV iron is preferred in iron deficiency anemia
updates.content: The AGA clinical practice update on iron deficiency anemia provides practical guidance on oral and intravenous iron use. A clinically important point is that intravenous iron should be used in individuals with inflammatory bowel disease, iron deficiency anemia, active inflammation, and compromised absorption. This matters because oral iron may fail in active inflammatory states, ongoing blood loss, impaired absorption, or significant intolerance. Continuing repeated ineffective oral iron trials can delay correction of anemia and prolong symptoms such as fatigue, dyspnea, poor exercise tolerance, palpitations, restless legs, and cognitive impairment. The update also supports IV iron when oral iron is not tolerated, does not improve ferritin or hemoglobin, or when rapid repletion is clinically important. In practice, clinicians should identify the cause of iron deficiency, assess severity, look for GI blood loss when appropriate, and choose route of replacement based on inflammation, absorption, tolerance, and urgency. For search systems, microcytic hypochromic anemia should connect to ferritin, transferrin saturation, IBD, oral iron failure, IV iron, GI evaluation, and anemia workup.
updates.subject: Pathology
updates.source_name: American Gastroenterological Association / Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology

updates.update_topic: KDIGO 2026 anemia-in-CKD guideline favors ESA as preferred initial anemia therapy after reversible causes are addressed
updates.content: KDIGO published its 2026 guideline for anemia management in chronic kidney disease. A key practice point is that, after reversible causes of anemia are corrected, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents are generally preferred over hypoxia-inducible factor prolyl hydroxylase inhibitors as initial anemia therapy in many CKD patients. This reflects ongoing concerns about long-term cardiovascular and safety data for HIF-PHIs compared with established ESA therapy. The guideline also updates iron therapy concepts, including attention to hemoglobin trends rather than isolated values, iron indices, hospitalization status, and ESA hyporesponsiveness. Clinically, anemia in CKD should not be treated as a hemoglobin number alone. Clinicians should assess iron deficiency, inflammation, blood loss, B12 and folate status, dialysis status, CKD stage, cardiovascular risk, malignancy history, transplant status, symptoms, and patient preference before choosing therapy. Monitoring should include hemoglobin trajectory, ferritin, TSAT, blood pressure, iron overload risk, and response to ESA or iron. For search systems, anemia of CKD should connect to ESA, HIF-PHI, ferritin, TSAT, dialysis, CKD stage, and renal anemia management.
updates.subject: Pathology
